title: EU AI Liability Directive 2026 — What Deployers Must Know Before 2027
context: 2026-08-27 EAT cycle — the revised AI Liability Directive (AILD) entered trilogue negotiations in May 2026; the compromise text published August 2026 retains the rebuttable presumption of causality and the disclosure-of-evidence mechanism. Transposition deadline expected December 2027.
body: The EU AI Liability Directive (AILD), revised and re-tabled in Q1 2026 following the Parliament's first-reading amendments, reached trilogue in May 2026. The August 2026 compromise text — likely the final shape — retains two provisions that change the liability landscape for every AI deployee operating in the EU: (1) a rebuttable presumption of causality: if a claimant shows that the deployee failed to comply with a relevant duty under the AI Act (risk management, human oversight, transparency, data governance) and the AI system's output caused harm, the court presumes the failure caused the harm unless the deployee proves otherwise; (2) a disclosure-of-evidence mechanism: the claimant can petition the court for disclosure of the deployee's documentation, logs, and measurement records, and the court shall order it unless the deployee shows the request is disproportionate. For a verification-first operator, the AILD turns measurement records from a compliance exercise into a liability defence: a signed, timestamped, auditable measurement record — showing instrumented boundaries, tested failure modes, and human-in-the-loop decision logs — is the evidence the deployee produces to rebut the presumption. The posture is monitored containment as legal architecture: the deployee who can prove they measured, detected, and contained is protected; the deployee who cannot faces the presumption.
